front: Chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell during <u>     </u>.
back: Chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell during **metaphase**.

front: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell during <u>     </u>.
back: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles of the cell during **anaphase**.

front: How does the behaviour of the **cell surface membrane** during division differ between animal and plant cells?
back:
In **animal cells**, the cell surface membrane **pinches inwards** to divide the cell.

In **plant cells**, a **new cell wall (cell plate)** forms across the middle instead.

front: Why are **root tips** used to observe mitosis?
back: The tip of a root contains a region of **actively dividing cells**, so many cells are caught in the process of **mitosis**.

front: How can you identify which **stage of mitosis** a cell is in?
back: By the **position and appearance of the chromosomes**, e.g. chromosomes lined up along the equator indicate **metaphase**.

front: In a photomicrograph, how would you identify a cell in **anaphase**?
back: The **chromatids are separating** and being pulled towards **opposite poles** of the cell.

front: Outline how to prepare a **root tip squash** to observe mitosis.
back:
**Cut** the tip from a growing root.

**Stain** it so the chromosomes become visible.

**Squash** the tip on a slide to spread the cells into a single layer.

View under a **microscope**.

front: The actively dividing cells used to observe mitosis are found in the <u>  </u> of a root.
back: The actively dividing cells used to observe mitosis are found in the **tip** of a root.

front:
**True or False?**

Most cells in a root tip sample are in mitosis at any one time.
back:
**False.**

Most cells are in **interphase**; only a small proportion are actively undergoing mitosis at any one time.

front: Define **nucleotide**.
back: A **nucleotide** is made of a **phosphate group**, a **pentose sugar** and a **nitrogenous base**.

front: What are the **three components** of a nucleotide?
back:
A **phosphate group**

A **pentose sugar**

A **nitrogenous base**

front: Describe the structure of **ATP**.
back:
**ATP** is a **phosphorylated nucleotide**.

It consists of the base **adenine**, the pentose sugar **ribose** and **three phosphate groups**.

front: Which two bases are **purines**?
back: **Adenine** and **guanine** are purines, and they have a **double ring** structure.

front: Which three bases are **pyrimidines**?
back: **Cytosine**, **thymine** and **uracil** are pyrimidines, and they have a **single ring** structure.

front: Adenine and guanine are purines with a <u>    </u> ring structure.
back: Adenine and guanine are purines with a **double** ring structure.

front:
**True or False?**

Thymine and uracil are both purines.
back:
**False.**

**Thymine** and **uracil** are **pyrimidines**, with a **single ring** structure.

front: What does it mean that the two DNA strands are **antiparallel**?
back:
The two strands run in **opposite directions**.

One runs **5' to 3'** and the other runs **3' to 5'**.

front: What are the **complementary base pairing** rules in DNA?
back:
**Adenine (A)** pairs with **thymine (T)**.

**Cytosine (C)** pairs with **guanine (G)**.

front: How does the **hydrogen bonding** differ between C–G and A–T base pairs?
back:
**C–G** pairs are joined by **three hydrogen bonds**.

**A–T** pairs are joined by **two hydrogen bonds**.

front: Which bonds link the nucleotides along a single DNA strand?
back: **Phosphodiester bonds** link adjacent nucleotides, joining the **phosphate** of one to the **sugar** of the next.

front: The two strands of a DNA molecule are twisted into a <u>    </u> helix.
back: The two strands of a DNA molecule are twisted into a **double** helix.

front:
**True or False?**

C–G base pairs are held together by two hydrogen bonds.
back:
**False.**

C–G pairs are held by **three** hydrogen bonds; A–T pairs are held by two.

front: What is **semi-conservative replication**?
back: DNA replication in which each new DNA molecule contains **one original (template) strand** and **one newly synthesised strand**.

front: During which stage of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur?
back: The **S phase** (synthesis phase) of interphase.

front: What is the role of **DNA polymerase** in replication?
back:
It catalyses the addition of new nucleotides to the growing strand by **complementary base pairing**.

It can only add nucleotides in the **5' to 3'** direction.

front: What is the role of **DNA ligase** in replication?
back: It **joins** the fragments of the **lagging strand** together by forming bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone.

front: Why is the **leading strand** made continuously but the **lagging strand** in fragments?
back:
DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the **5' to 3'** direction.

The **leading strand** is synthesised continuously towards the replication fork.

The **lagging strand** is synthesised in short fragments away from the fork.

front: Replication is described as <u>          </u> because each new molecule keeps one original strand.
back: Replication is described as **semi-conservative** because each new molecule keeps one original strand.

front: Give **three differences** between an RNA molecule and a DNA molecule.
back:
RNA is **single-stranded**; DNA is double-stranded.

RNA contains the sugar **ribose**; DNA contains deoxyribose.

RNA contains the base **uracil**; DNA contains thymine.

front: What is **mRNA (messenger RNA)**?
back: A **single-stranded** RNA molecule that carries a copy of the genetic code from the **DNA** to the **ribosomes**.

front: Which pentose sugar is found in an RNA molecule?
back: **Ribose**.

front: In RNA, the base uracil replaces the base <u>    </u> found in DNA.
back: In RNA, the base uracil replaces the base **thymine** found in DNA.

front:
**True or False?**

An mRNA molecule is double-stranded.
back:
**False.**

mRNA is **single-stranded**.

front: Define **gene**.
back: A **gene** is a sequence of **nucleotides** that forms part of a **DNA molecule** and codes for a **polypeptide**.

front: What does a **gene** code for?
back: A **polypeptide**.

front: A gene is a sequence of <u>       </u> that forms part of a DNA molecule.
back: A gene is a sequence of **nucleotides** that forms part of a DNA molecule.

front:
**True or False?**

A polypeptide is coded for by a gene.
back:
**True.**

A gene is the sequence of DNA nucleotides that codes for a polypeptide.

front: What is the **genetic code**?
back: The set of **DNA base triplets** that code for specific **amino acids**, or for **start and stop** signals.

front: Why is the genetic code described as **universal**?
back: The **same triplet** codes for the **same amino acid** in almost all living organisms.

front: What can a **triplet** of DNA bases code for?
back:
A specific **amino acid**.

Or a **start** or **stop** codon.

front: A sequence of three DNA bases that codes for one amino acid is called a <u>    </u>.
back: A sequence of three DNA bases that codes for one amino acid is called a **triplet**.

front:
**True or False?**

Some base triplets act as start and stop codons rather than coding for an amino acid.
back:
**True.**

Start and stop codons signal where translation begins and ends.

front: Define **transcription**.
back: The process in which a complementary **mRNA** copy is made from a **DNA template strand**.

front: Define **translation**.
back: The process in which the sequence of **codons** on mRNA is used to assemble **amino acids** into a polypeptide at a **ribosome**.

front: What is the role of **RNA polymerase**?
back: It joins RNA nucleotides together to form **mRNA** during **transcription**.

front: What is the role of **tRNA (transfer RNA)**?
back:
It carries a specific **amino acid** to the ribosome.

Its **anticodon** pairs with the complementary **codon** on mRNA.

front: What is the role of the **ribosome** in translation?
back: It holds the **mRNA** and **tRNA** in place so that **peptide bonds** form between adjacent amino acids.

front: What is the difference between a **codon** and an **anticodon**?
back:
A **codon** is a triplet of bases on **mRNA**.

An **anticodon** is the complementary triplet of bases on **tRNA**.

front: During translation, mRNA carries codons to a <u>     </u> where the polypeptide is assembled.
back: During translation, mRNA carries codons to a **ribosome** where the polypeptide is assembled.

front: What is the **template strand**?
back:
The DNA strand that is **used** during transcription to make mRNA.

It is also called the **transcribed strand**.

front: What is the DNA strand that is **not used** in transcription called?
back: The **non-transcribed strand**.

front: The DNA strand used during transcription is called the template or <u>       </u> strand.
back: The DNA strand used during transcription is called the template or **transcribed** strand.

front: What is an **intron**?
back: A **non-coding** sequence that is **removed** from the primary transcript during modification.

front: What is an **exon**?
back: A **coding** sequence that is **joined** to other exons to form the final mRNA.

front: In eukaryotes, how is the primary transcript modified to form mRNA?
back:
The **introns** (non-coding sequences) are **removed**.

The **exons** (coding sequences) are **joined** together.

front: In eukaryotes, non-coding sequences called <u>    </u> are removed to form mRNA.
back: In eukaryotes, non-coding sequences called **introns** are removed to form mRNA.

front: What is a **gene mutation**?
back: A **change** in the sequence of **base pairs** in a DNA molecule that may result in an **altered polypeptide**.

front: What are the **three types** of gene mutation?
back:
**Substitution**

**Deletion**

**Insertion**

front: How can a **substitution** mutation affect the polypeptide?
back:
One base is replaced by another, changing **only one triplet**.

So at most **one amino acid** is altered — and sometimes none, because the code is degenerate.

front: Why do **deletion** and **insertion** mutations often have a large effect?
back:
They cause a **frameshift**.

Every triplet **after** the mutation is changed, so **many amino acids** in the polypeptide may be altered.

front: A change in the sequence of base pairs in DNA is called a gene <u>     </u>.
back: A change in the sequence of base pairs in DNA is called a gene **mutation**.

front:
**True or False?**

A substitution mutation always changes the polypeptide produced.
back:
**False.**

The genetic code is degenerate, so the new triplet may still code for the **same amino acid**.

front: Define **plan diagram**.
back: A **plan diagram** shows the **distribution of tissues** in a section, with **no individual cells** drawn.

front: What are the rules for drawing a **plan diagram** (tissue map) of a transverse section?
back:
Draw only the **outlines** of tissues.

Do **not** draw individual cells.

Keep tissues in the correct **proportions**, with no shading.

front: What is a **herbaceous dicotyledonous** plant?
back: A **non-woody** plant whose seeds contain **two cotyledons** (seed leaves).

front: Which three plant organs should you be able to draw in **transverse section**?
back: The **stem**, the **root** and the **leaf**.

front: A plan diagram shows the <u>       </u> of tissues but not individual cells.
back: A plan diagram shows the **distribution** of tissues but not individual cells.

front:
**True or False?**

Individual cells should be drawn on a plan diagram.
back:
**False.**

A plan diagram shows only the outlines and distribution of tissues, never individual cells.

front: Describe the distribution of **xylem** and **phloem** in a **root**.
back:
The **xylem** is in the **centre**, in a star or cross shape.

The **phloem** sits **between the arms** of the xylem.

front: Describe the distribution of **xylem** and **phloem** in a **stem**.
back:
They are in **vascular bundles** arranged in a **ring** near the outside.

In each bundle the **xylem** is on the **inside** and the **phloem** on the **outside**.

front: Describe the distribution of **xylem** and **phloem** in a **leaf**.
back:
They are in **vascular bundles** in the **midrib** and **veins**.

The **xylem** lies **above** the **phloem**.

front:
**True or False?**

In a stem, the phloem is found inside the xylem.
back:
**False.**

In a **stem** the **xylem** is on the **inside** of each vascular bundle and the **phloem** on the **outside**.

front: Define **vascular bundle**.
back: A **vascular bundle** is a strand of transport tissue containing both **xylem** and **phloem**.

front: Describe the distribution of **xylem and phloem** in a dicotyledonous **stem**.
back:
Vascular bundles are arranged in a **ring** near the outer edge.

In each bundle the **xylem** is towards the inside and the **phloem** towards the outside.

front: Describe the distribution of **xylem and phloem** in a dicotyledonous **root**.
back:
The vascular tissue is in the **centre** of the root.

The **xylem** forms a central **X (star) shape**, with **phloem** between its arms.

front: Describe the distribution of **xylem and phloem** in a dicotyledonous **leaf**.
back:
Vascular bundles run through the **midrib** and **veins**.

The **xylem** lies on the **upper** side and the **phloem** on the **lower** side of each bundle.

front: In a dicotyledonous root, the xylem and phloem are found in the <u>    </u> of the root.
back: In a dicotyledonous root, the xylem and phloem are found in the **centre** of the root.

front: In a dicotyledonous stem, the vascular bundles are arranged in a <u>  </u> near the outer edge.
back: In a dicotyledonous stem, the vascular bundles are arranged in a **ring** near the outer edge.

front: Define **xylem**.
back: **Xylem** is the tissue that transports **water** and **mineral ions** from the roots up the plant, and provides **support**.

front: Describe the structure of a **xylem vessel element**.
back:
It is a **dead, empty** cell with **no cytoplasm** or organelles.

The **end walls** have broken down to form a continuous hollow tube (lumen).

The walls are thickened with **lignin** and contain **pits**.

front: Relate the structure of a **xylem vessel** to its function.
back:
**No end walls** and no cytoplasm give an uninterrupted, low-resistance column for **water flow**.

**Lignin** strengthens the walls, giving support and stopping them collapsing under tension.

**Pits** allow water to move sideways between vessels.

front: Define **lignin**.
back: **Lignin** is a strong, **waterproof** substance that thickens and strengthens xylem cell walls.

front: What are **pits** and why are they important in xylem vessels?
back:
**Pits** are non-lignified gaps in the vessel wall.

They allow water to move **sideways** between neighbouring vessels.

front: Xylem vessel walls are strengthened and waterproofed by <u>    </u>.
back: Xylem vessel walls are strengthened and waterproofed by **lignin**.

front:
**True or False?**

Xylem vessel elements are living cells.
back:
**False.**

Xylem vessel elements are dead and empty, with no cytoplasm, which allows free water flow.

front: Define **phloem**.
back: **Phloem** is the living tissue that transports **assimilates**, such as **sucrose** and **amino acids**, around the plant.

front: Describe the structure of a **sieve tube element**.
back:
A **living** cell with **little cytoplasm** and **no nucleus**.

Its **end walls** form perforated **sieve plates**.

The cells are joined end to end into a continuous **tube**.

front: Define **sieve plate**.
back: A **sieve plate** is the perforated **end wall** between sieve tube elements, whose pores allow **sap** to flow through.

front: How is a **companion cell** adapted to its function?
back:
It has **dense cytoplasm** and many **mitochondria**.

These provide the **ATP** needed to actively load sucrose into the phloem and to carry out the metabolism of the sieve tube element.

front: Why do **sieve tube elements** need **companion cells**?
back:
Sieve tube elements have **no nucleus** and few organelles.

The companion cell carries out the **metabolic functions** that keep the sieve tube element alive and working.

front: The perforated end walls between sieve tube elements are called <u>       </u>.
back: The perforated end walls between sieve tube elements are called **sieve plates**.

front: Companion cells contain many <u>       </u> to provide ATP for loading sucrose.
back: Companion cells contain many **mitochondria** to provide ATP for loading sucrose.

front: How is the structure of a **sieve tube element** related to its function?
back:
It has **no nucleus** and only a **thin layer of cytoplasm** around the edge.

This maximises space and reduces friction, allowing **assimilates (sap)** to flow through with little resistance.

front: How are **mineral ions** and **organic compounds** transported within a plant?
back: They are **dissolved in water** and carried through the plant.

front: Define the **apoplast pathway**.
back: The **apoplast pathway** is the movement of water through the **cellulose cell walls** and intercellular spaces, without entering the cytoplasm.

front: Define the **symplast pathway**.
back: The **symplast pathway** is the movement of water through the **cytoplasm** of cells, passing from cell to cell through **plasmodesmata**.

front: Define the **Casparian strip**.
back: The **Casparian strip** is a waterproof band of **suberin** in the cell walls of the **endodermis**.

front: What is the role of the **Casparian strip** at the endodermis?
back:
The **suberin** in the Casparian strip is **waterproof**.

It blocks the **apoplast pathway**, forcing water into the **symplast pathway** to cross the endodermis.

front: The apoplast pathway carries water through the cellulose cell <u>   </u>.
back: The apoplast pathway carries water through the cellulose cell **walls**.

front: At the endodermis, the Casparian strip is made waterproof by <u>    </u>.
back: At the endodermis, the Casparian strip is made waterproof by **suberin**.

front:
**True or False?**

In the apoplast pathway, water moves through the cytoplasm of cells.
back:
**False.**

In the apoplast pathway water moves through the cell walls; movement through the cytoplasm is the symplast pathway.

front: What is the role of **lignin** in the transport of water through a plant?
back:
**Lignin** waterproofs and strengthens the walls of the **xylem** vessels.

This stops water leaking out and stops the vessels collapsing under tension, helping to maintain the continuous **water column**.

front: Define **transpiration**.
back: **Transpiration** is the loss of **water vapour** from the leaves and aerial parts of a plant by **evaporation** and **diffusion**.

front: Describe the process of **transpiration**.
back:
Water **evaporates** from the internal surfaces of the mesophyll cells inside the leaf.

The water vapour collects in the **air spaces**.

It then **diffuses** out through the **stomata** to the atmosphere.

front: Why is transpiration described as **evaporation followed by diffusion**?
back:
Water first **evaporates** from the internal leaf surfaces into the air spaces.

The water vapour then **diffuses** out of the stomata to the atmosphere.

front: Water vapour diffuses out of the leaf through pores called <u>    </u>.
back: Water vapour diffuses out of the leaf through pores called **stomata**.

front: In transpiration, water <u>      </u> from the internal surfaces of the leaf.
back: In transpiration, water **evaporates** from the internal surfaces of the leaf.

front:
**True or False?**

Transpiration only involves the evaporation of water.
back:
**False.**

Transpiration involves evaporation of water from internal leaf surfaces followed by diffusion of water vapour to the atmosphere.

front: Define **cohesion** (of water).
back: **Cohesion** is the attraction between water molecules caused by **hydrogen bonding**.

front: Define **adhesion** (of water in the xylem).
back: **Adhesion** is the attraction between water molecules and the **cellulose** cell walls of the xylem.

front: Define **transpiration pull**.
back: **Transpiration pull** is the **tension** that draws water up the xylem, created by water loss from the leaves.

front: Explain the **cohesion-tension** theory of water movement in the xylem.
back:
Water lost by transpiration creates a **tension** (pull) at the top of the xylem.

**Hydrogen bonds** hold water molecules together by **cohesion**, forming a continuous column.

The whole column is pulled up the xylem, aided by **adhesion** to the cellulose walls.

front: How does **hydrogen bonding** help water move up the xylem?
back:
Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together (**cohesion**).

This keeps the water column **continuous** so it does not break as it is pulled up.

front: The attraction between water molecules, caused by hydrogen bonding, is called <u>     </u>.
back: The attraction between water molecules, caused by hydrogen bonding, is called **cohesion**.

front: The attraction between water molecules and the xylem cell walls is called <u>     </u>.
back: The attraction between water molecules and the xylem cell walls is called **adhesion**.

front: Define **xerophyte**.
back: A **xerophyte** is a plant **adapted** to live in **dry conditions** where water is limited.

front: How do **sunken stomata** reduce water loss in a xerophyte?
back:
They trap **humid air** in pits next to the stomata.

This reduces the **water potential gradient**, so less water vapour diffuses out.

front: How does a **thick waxy cuticle** reduce water loss?
back:
It forms a **waterproof** barrier over the leaf surface.

This reduces **evaporation** of water directly through the epidermis.

front: How do **rolled leaves** reduce transpiration in a xerophyte?
back:
Rolling traps **humid air** inside the leaf.

This lowers the water potential gradient and reduces the **surface area** exposed to the air.

front: How do **hairs (trichomes)** on a leaf reduce water loss?
back:
They trap a layer of **humid air** close to the stomata.

This reduces the **water potential gradient**, slowing diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf.

front: A thick waxy <u>    </u> reduces evaporation from the leaf surface.
back: A thick waxy **cuticle** reduces evaporation from the leaf surface.

front: Sunken stomata and leaf hairs both trap <u>   </u> air to reduce the water potential gradient.
back: Sunken stomata and leaf hairs both trap **humid** air to reduce the water potential gradient.

front: Define **assimilates**.
back: **Assimilates** are organic substances made by the plant, such as **sucrose** and **amino acids**.

front: Define **source** (in phloem transport).
back: A **source** is a part of the plant that **loads** assimilates into the phloem, such as a photosynthesising **leaf**.

front: Define **sink** (in phloem transport).
back: A **sink** is a part of the plant that **removes** assimilates from the phloem, such as a **root** or a growing region.

front: Which **assimilates** are transported in the phloem, and where do they move?
back:
**Sucrose** and **amino acids**, dissolved in water.

They move from **sources** to **sinks** in the phloem sieve tubes.

front: Assimilates move through the phloem sieve tubes from sources to <u>   </u>.
back: Assimilates move through the phloem sieve tubes from sources to **sinks**.

front:
**True or False?**

Sucrose is transported in the xylem.
back:
**False.**

Sucrose and other assimilates are transported in the phloem; the xylem carries water and mineral ions.

front: Explain how **sucrose is loaded** into the phloem at the source.
back:
**Proton pumps** use **ATP** to actively pump **H^+^** ions out of the companion cell.

This builds up a high concentration of H<sup>+</sup> outside the cell.

The H<sup>+</sup> ions diffuse back in through **cotransporter proteins**, bringing **sucrose** with them.

Sucrose then passes into the sieve tube element.

front: Define **cotransporter protein** (in sucrose loading).
back: A **cotransporter protein** is a membrane protein that moves **H^+^** ions and **sucrose** together into the companion cell.

front: What is the role of the **proton pump** in sucrose loading?
back:
It uses **ATP** to actively pump **H^+^** ions out of the companion cell.

This sets up the H<sup>+</sup> concentration gradient that drives sucrose uptake.

front: Why do companion cells contain many **mitochondria**?
back: To produce the **ATP** needed for the **active transport** of H<sup>+</sup> ions by the proton pumps during sucrose loading.

front: Sucrose loading uses <u>    </u> pumps to move H<sup>+</sup> ions out of the companion cell.
back: Sucrose loading uses **proton** pumps to move H<sup>+</sup> ions out of the companion cell.

front: H<sup>+</sup> ions re-enter the companion cell together with sucrose through <u>        </u> proteins.
back: H<sup>+</sup> ions re-enter the companion cell together with sucrose through **cotransporter** proteins.

front:
**True or False?**

Loading sucrose into the phloem is a passive process.
back:
**False.**

It requires ATP to power the proton pumps, so it is an active process.

front: Define **mass flow** (in phloem).
back: **Mass flow** is the bulk movement of phloem sap down a **hydrostatic pressure gradient** from **source** to **sink**.

front: How is a high **hydrostatic pressure** created at the **source**?
back:
**Sucrose** is loaded into the sieve tube, **lowering** its water potential.

Water then enters from the xylem by **osmosis**.

This raises the **hydrostatic pressure** in the sieve tube at the source.

front: How is the **hydrostatic pressure** lowered at the **sink**?
back:
**Sucrose** is unloaded from the sieve tube, **raising** its water potential.

Water then leaves the phloem by **osmosis**.

This **lowers** the hydrostatic pressure at the sink.

front: In which direction does phloem sap move by **mass flow**?
back: From the **high** hydrostatic pressure at the **source** to the **low** hydrostatic pressure at the **sink**.

front: In mass flow, phloem sap moves down a <u>       </u> pressure gradient.
back: In mass flow, phloem sap moves down a **hydrostatic** pressure gradient.

front: Water enters the sieve tube at the source by <u>    </u>, raising the hydrostatic pressure.
back: Water enters the sieve tube at the source by **osmosis**, raising the hydrostatic pressure.

front:
**True or False?**

In mass flow, phloem sap moves from the sink to the source.
back:
**False.**

Phloem sap moves from source to sink, down a hydrostatic pressure gradient.

front: Define **closed circulatory system**.
back: In a **closed circulatory system**, blood is always contained within **blood vessels** and the heart, and does not directly bathe the tissues.

front: Define **double circulation**.
back: In a **double circulation**, blood passes through the **heart twice** for each complete circuit of the body.

front: Name the **two circuits** of the mammalian double circulation.
back:
The **pulmonary circulation** — between the heart and the lungs.

The **systemic circulation** — between the heart and the rest of the body.

front: List the **five types of blood vessel** blood flows through, in order away from the heart.
back: **Arteries** → **arterioles** → **capillaries** → **venules** → **veins**.

front: The mammalian circulatory system is a closed <u>    </u> circulation.
back: The mammalian circulatory system is a closed **double** circulation.

front:
**True or False?**

In a double circulation, blood passes through the heart once per circuit.
back:
**False.**

Blood passes through the heart **twice** for each complete circuit of the body.

front: What is the function of the **pulmonary artery**?
back: It carries **deoxygenated** blood from the heart (right ventricle) to the **lungs**.

front: What is the function of the **pulmonary vein**?
back: It carries **oxygenated** blood from the **lungs** back to the heart (left atrium).

front: What is the function of the **aorta**?
back: It carries **oxygenated** blood from the heart (left ventricle) to the **body**.

front: What is the function of the **vena cava**?
back: It carries **deoxygenated** blood from the **body** back to the heart (right atrium).

front: Which two vessels make up the **pulmonary circulation**?
back: The **pulmonary artery** (heart → lungs) and the **pulmonary vein** (lungs → heart).

front: Unusually, the pulmonary <u>    </u> carries deoxygenated blood.
back: Unusually, the pulmonary **artery** carries deoxygenated blood.

front: How can you recognise an **artery** in a transverse section?
back: It has a **thick wall** and a relatively **small, round lumen**, often with a folded (wavy) inner lining.

front: How can you recognise a **vein** in a transverse section?
back: It has a **thin wall** and a **large, irregular lumen**.

front: How can you recognise a **capillary**?
back: It has a **wall one cell thick** and a lumen just wide enough for a single **red blood cell**.

front: Define a **plan diagram**.
back: A **plan diagram** is a low-power drawing showing the **outlines of tissues**, with no individual cells drawn.

front: A plan diagram shows the outlines of tissues but never individual <u>   </u>.
back: A plan diagram shows the outlines of tissues but never individual **cells**.

front: In which two planes can a blood vessel be **sectioned** to draw a plan diagram?
back:
**Transverse section (TS)** — a cross-section across the vessel.

**Longitudinal section (LS)** — a lengthways section along the vessel.

front: How is the structure of an **elastic artery** related to its function?
back:
Its wall contains much **elastic tissue** that **stretches and recoils**.

This smooths out the high-pressure surges from the heart, maintaining a steadier blood flow.

front: How is the structure of a **muscular artery** related to its function?
back:
Its wall contains **smooth muscle** that contracts and relaxes.

This controls the volume of blood distributed to different organs.

front: How is the structure of a **vein** related to its function?
back:
It has a **thin wall**, a **wide lumen** and **valves**.

This returns blood to the heart at low pressure, with the valves preventing backflow.

front: How is the structure of a **capillary** related to its function?
back:
Its wall is only **one cell thick**, giving a **short diffusion distance**.

This allows efficient exchange of substances between the blood and tissues.

front: Define the **endothelium**.
back: The **endothelium** is the smooth, single layer of cells that **lines** all blood vessels, reducing friction with the blood.

front: <u>    </u> in the veins prevent the backflow of blood.
back: **Valves** in the veins prevent the backflow of blood.

front: How do you recognise a **red blood cell**?
back: It is a small **biconcave disc** with **no nucleus**.

front: How do you recognise a **neutrophil**?
back: It has a **multi-lobed nucleus** and **granular** cytoplasm.

front: How do you recognise a **lymphocyte**?
back: It has a **large, round nucleus** that fills most of the cell, with only a thin rim of cytoplasm.

front: How do you recognise a **monocyte**?
back: It is the **largest** white blood cell and has a **bean-shaped (kidney-shaped) nucleus**.

front: A red blood cell has no <u>    </u>, leaving more room for haemoglobin.
back: A red blood cell has no **nucleus**, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

front: <u>   </u> is the main component of both blood and tissue fluid.
back: **Water** is the main component of both blood and tissue fluid.

front: How does the **solvent action** of water help transport in mammals?
back:
Many substances (such as glucose, ions and oxygen) **dissolve** in water.

This allows them to be carried in solution in the blood plasma.

front: How does the **high specific heat capacity** of water help mammals?
back:
Water **resists changes in temperature**.

This lets the blood distribute heat around the body and helps keep body temperature stable.

front: Define **specific heat capacity**.
back: **Specific heat capacity** is the energy needed to raise the temperature of a substance by a given amount; water's is **high**, so it warms and cools slowly.

front:
**True or False?**

Water is a poor solvent, which limits transport in the blood.
back:
**False.**

Water is an **excellent solvent**, allowing many substances to be transported dissolved in the plasma.

front: Define **tissue fluid**.
back: **Tissue fluid** is the fluid that surrounds and bathes the body's cells, formed from **blood plasma**.

front: State the **functions of tissue fluid**.
back:
It supplies cells with **oxygen, glucose and other nutrients**.

It removes **waste products** (such as carbon dioxide) from cells.

It acts as the medium of exchange between the blood and the cells.

front: How is tissue fluid **formed** at the arterial end of a capillary?
back:
The high **hydrostatic pressure** forces plasma (without large proteins and cells) out through the capillary wall.

This is called **ultrafiltration**.

front: Why does water **return** to the capillary at the venous end?
back:
Hydrostatic pressure has fallen, and the remaining **plasma proteins** give the blood a **low water potential**.

So water re-enters the capillary by **osmosis**.

front: Excess tissue fluid that is not reabsorbed drains into the <u>     </u> system.
back: Excess tissue fluid that is not reabsorbed drains into the **lymphatic** system.

front: How is **oxygen** transported by red blood cells?
back:
Oxygen binds to **haemoglobin** to form **oxyhaemoglobin**.

Each haemoglobin molecule can carry up to **four** oxygen molecules.

front: Define **carbonic anhydrase**.
back: **Carbonic anhydrase** is an enzyme in red blood cells that catalyses the reaction of **carbon dioxide with water** to form carbonic acid.

front: How does **carbonic anhydrase** help transport carbon dioxide?
back:
It catalyses: CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>

The carbonic acid then dissociates into **H^+^** ions and **hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO~3~^-^)**.

front: What is **haemoglobinic acid** and how does it form?
back:
The **H^+^** ions released from carbonic acid bind to **haemoglobin**, forming **haemoglobinic acid**.

This buffers the H<sup>+</sup>, preventing a harmful fall in blood pH.

front: Define **carbaminohaemoglobin**.
back: **Carbaminohaemoglobin** is the compound formed when **carbon dioxide binds directly** to haemoglobin.

front: The enzyme carbonic <u>     </u> speeds up the reaction of carbon dioxide with water.
back: The enzyme carbonic **anhydrase** speeds up the reaction of carbon dioxide with water.

front:
**True or False?**

Most carbon dioxide is carried bound directly to haemoglobin.
back:
**False.**

Most carbon dioxide is carried as **hydrogencarbonate ions**; only some binds directly as **carbaminohaemoglobin**.

front: Define the **chloride shift**.
back: The **chloride shift** is the movement of **chloride ions (Cl^-^) into** the red blood cell as **hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO~3~^-^) diffuse out**.

front: Why does the **chloride shift** occur?
back: As **HCO~3~^-^** ions diffuse out of the red blood cell into the plasma, **Cl^-^** ions move in to **balance the charge**.

front: Why is the **chloride shift** important?
back:
It **maintains the electrical neutrality** of the red blood cell.

This allows carbon dioxide to keep being transported efficiently.

front: During the chloride shift, <u>     </u> ions move into the red blood cell.
back: During the chloride shift, **chloride** ions move into the red blood cell.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydrogencarbonate ions move into the red blood cell during the chloride shift.
back:
**False.**

Hydrogencarbonate ions move **out** of the red blood cell; chloride ions move **in**.

front: In what **three ways** is carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
back:
As **hydrogencarbonate ions** in the plasma (most).

As **carbaminohaemoglobin** (bound to haemoglobin).

**Dissolved** directly in the plasma (a small amount).

front: What is the **main form** in which carbon dioxide is carried in the plasma?
back: As **hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO~3~^-^)**.

front: How do **hydrogencarbonate ions** come to be in the plasma?
back:
Inside red blood cells, CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, which dissociates into H<sup>+</sup> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>.

The **HCO~3~^-^** ions then diffuse **out into the plasma**.

front: What happens to plasma **hydrogencarbonate ions** at the lungs?
back:
They re-enter the red blood cells and recombine with H<sup>+</sup> to form **carbon dioxide and water**.

The carbon dioxide is then **exhaled**.

front: Most carbon dioxide is transported in the plasma as <u>          </u> ions.
back: Most carbon dioxide is transported in the plasma as **hydrogencarbonate** ions.

front: Define the **partial pressure of oxygen (pO~2~)**.
back: The **partial pressure of oxygen** is a measure of the concentration of oxygen present — the pressure it contributes in a mixture of gases.

front: Describe the **shape** of the oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin.
back: It is **S-shaped (sigmoid)**.

front: The oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin is <u>    </u> in shape.
back: The oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin is **sigmoid** in shape.

front: **Explain** why the oxygen dissociation curve is S-shaped.
back:
Binding of the **first oxygen** changes the shape of haemoglobin (a conformational change).

This makes it **easier** for the next oxygen molecules to bind — known as **cooperative binding**.

front: What does the curve show at the **high pO~2~** found in the lungs?
back: Haemoglobin has a **high affinity** for oxygen and becomes **almost fully saturated** — it **loads** oxygen.

front: What does the curve show at the **low pO~2~** found in respiring tissues?
back: Haemoglobin has a **lower affinity** for oxygen and its saturation falls — it **unloads (releases)** oxygen to the tissues.

front: Define the **Bohr shift**.
back: The **Bohr shift** is the effect of an increased **carbon dioxide** concentration causing haemoglobin to **release oxygen more readily**.

front: In which **direction** does the oxygen dissociation curve move during the Bohr shift, and why?
back:
It shifts to the **right**.

Higher carbon dioxide lowers haemoglobin's **affinity** for oxygen.

front: How does **carbon dioxide** cause the Bohr shift?
back:
Carbon dioxide forms **carbonic acid**, releasing **H^+^** ions.

The H<sup>+</sup> ions bind to haemoglobin, lowering its affinity for oxygen so more oxygen is released.

front: Why is the **Bohr shift** important?
back:
In actively respiring tissues, carbon dioxide levels are high.

The Bohr shift means **more oxygen is unloaded** exactly where it is most needed.

front: During the Bohr shift, the oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the <u>   </u>.
back: During the Bohr shift, the oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the **right**.

front: Name the **four chambers** of the heart.
back:
The left and right **atria** (upper chambers).

The left and right **ventricles** (lower chambers).

front: Which blood vessels connect to the **right** side of the heart?
back: The **vena cava** (into the right atrium) and the **pulmonary artery** (out of the right ventricle).

front: Which blood vessels connect to the **left** side of the heart?
back: The **pulmonary vein** (into the left atrium) and the **aorta** (out of the left ventricle).

front: Define the **septum**.
back: The **septum** is the muscular wall separating the left and right sides of the heart, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.

front: What is the function of the **coronary arteries**?
back: They lie on the surface of the heart and supply the **heart muscle** itself with **oxygenated blood**.

front: Name the **atrioventricular valves** on each side of the heart.
back:
The **tricuspid valve** on the right side.

The **bicuspid (mitral) valve** on the left side.

front: Why are the **ventricle** walls thicker than the **atrial** walls?
back:
The **ventricles** pump blood much further, so they need more **muscle** to generate a higher **pressure**.

The **atria** only pump blood into the ventricles just below them.

front: Why is the **left ventricle** wall thicker than the **right**?
back:
The **left ventricle** pumps blood around the **whole body**, so it must generate a much higher **pressure**.

The **right ventricle** only pumps to the **lungs**, which are close by and would be damaged by high pressure.

front: The muscular wall separating the left and right sides of the heart is the <u>          </u>.
back: The muscular wall separating the left and right sides of the heart is the **septum**.

front:
**True or False?**

The pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood away from the heart.
back:
**False.**

The **pulmonary artery** carries **deoxygenated** blood from the **right ventricle** to the lungs.

front: Why do the **ventricles** have thicker walls than the **atria**?
back:
The ventricles must generate a **higher pressure** to pump blood out of the heart.

The atria only pump blood a **short distance** into the ventricles.

front: Why is the wall of the **left ventricle** thicker than that of the **right ventricle**?
back:
The left ventricle pumps blood at **high pressure** all around the body (systemic circulation).

The right ventricle only pumps blood a short distance to the **lungs**, at lower pressure.

front: Why must the **right ventricle** pump blood at a **lower pressure**?
back: High pressure would **damage the delicate lung capillaries** and force out too much tissue fluid.

front: The <u>  </u> ventricle has the thickest muscular wall.
back: The **left** ventricle has the thickest muscular wall.

front:
**True or False?**

The atria have thicker walls than the ventricles.
back:
**False.**

The **ventricles** have thicker walls, as they pump blood at higher pressure.

front: Define the **cardiac cycle**.
back: The **cardiac cycle** is the sequence of events in one complete **heartbeat**.

front: Define **systole**.
back: **Systole** is the **contraction** of heart muscle.

front: Define **diastole**.
back: **Diastole** is the **relaxation** of heart muscle.

front: What happens during **atrial systole**?
back:
The **atria contract**, pushing the remaining blood into the ventricles.

The **atrioventricular valves are open**.

front: What happens to the valves during **ventricular systole**?
back:
Rising ventricular pressure closes the **atrioventricular valves**.

When ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, the **semilunar valves open** and blood is forced out.

front: What causes the **semilunar valves to close**?
back:
During **diastole**, ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure.

The higher arterial pressure pushes the semilunar valves shut, preventing backflow.

front: The contraction of heart muscle is called <u>    </u>.
back: The contraction of heart muscle is called **systole**.

front: Define the **sinoatrial node (SAN)**.
back: The **sinoatrial node** is the heart's **pacemaker**, in the wall of the right atrium, which sets the heart rate.

front: What is the role of the **sinoatrial node (SAN)**?
back: It generates a **wave of electrical excitation** that spreads across both **atria**, causing them to contract.

front: Define the **atrioventricular node (AVN)**.
back: The **atrioventricular node** lies between the atria and ventricles; it **delays** the impulse before passing it to the ventricles.

front: Why is there a **delay** at the atrioventricular node?
back: The delay ensures the **atria finish contracting** and empty completely **before** the ventricles contract.

front: What is the role of the **Purkyne tissue**?
back:
It conducts the wave of excitation down the **septum** to the **apex** of the heart.

This makes the ventricles contract from the **apex upwards**, pushing blood up towards the arteries.

front: The heart's pacemaker is the <u>      </u> node.
back: The heart's pacemaker is the **sinoatrial** node.

front: List the structures that make up the **human gas exchange system**.
back: The **lungs**, **trachea**, **bronchi**, **bronchioles**, **alveoli** and a surrounding **capillary network**.

front: Trace the path of air from the **trachea** to the site of gas exchange.
back: **Trachea** → **bronchi** → **bronchioles** → **alveoli**.

front: Define **trachea**.
back: The **trachea** is the main airway (windpipe) that carries air towards the lungs, dividing into two bronchi.

front: Define **bronchi**.
back: The **bronchi** are the two large airways that branch from the trachea, one leading into each lung.

front: Define **bronchioles**.
back: The **bronchioles** are the small airways that branch from the bronchi and lead to the alveoli.

front: Define **alveoli**.
back: The **alveoli** are the tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles, and are the site of gas exchange in the lungs.

front: What is the **capillary network** of the lungs?
back: A dense network of **capillaries** surrounding each alveolus, bringing blood close to the air for gas exchange.

front: The two large airways that branch from the trachea, one to each lung, are the <u>    </u>.
back: The two large airways that branch from the trachea, one to each lung, are the **bronchi**.

front:
**True or False?**

Gas exchange takes place in the bronchioles.
back:
**False.**

Gas exchange takes place in the **alveoli**; the **bronchioles** only carry air to them.

front: Where in the gas exchange system is **cartilage** found?
back: In the walls of the **trachea** (as C-shaped rings) and the **bronchi** (as irregular blocks). It is absent from the bronchioles and alveoli.

front: Where is **ciliated epithelium** found in the gas exchange system?
back: Lining the **trachea**, **bronchi** and larger **bronchioles**. It is not present in the alveoli.

front: Where are **goblet cells** found?
back: Scattered among the ciliated epithelium that lines the **trachea**, **bronchi** and larger **bronchioles**.

front: Where is the **squamous epithelium** of the gas exchange system found?
back: Forming the very thin walls of the **alveoli**.

front: Where is **smooth muscle** found in the gas exchange system?
back: In the walls of the **trachea**, **bronchi** and **bronchioles**.

front: Where are **capillaries** distributed in the gas exchange system?
back: In a dense network surrounding the **alveoli**.

front: The thin walls of the alveoli are made of <u>     </u> epithelium.
back: The thin walls of the alveoli are made of **squamous** epithelium.

front:
**True or False?**

Cartilage is found in the walls of the alveoli.
back:
**False.**

Cartilage is found only in the trachea and bronchi; the alveoli have thin walls of squamous epithelium.

front: How can you recognise **ciliated epithelium** in a photomicrograph?
back: Column-shaped (**columnar**) cells with tiny hair-like **cilia** projecting from their free surface.

front: How can you recognise a **goblet cell**?
back: A **goblet-shaped** cell with a pale, swollen top full of **mucus**, wedged between the ciliated cells.

front: How can you recognise **cartilage** in a slide?
back: A pale-staining supporting tissue containing cells sitting in spaces within a firm **matrix**.

front: How can you recognise the **squamous epithelium** of an alveolus?
back: Very **thin, flattened** cells forming a single, smooth layer.

front: How can you recognise **smooth muscle** in a section?
back: Sheets of **spindle-shaped** cells, each with a single elongated nucleus.

front: How can you recognise a **capillary** in a photomicrograph?
back: A very narrow vessel with a wall just **one cell thick**, often with a **red blood cell** in the lumen.

front: Epithelial cells that bear hair-like projections on their free surface are described as <u>     </u>.
back: Epithelial cells that bear hair-like projections on their free surface are described as **ciliated**.

front: How can you recognise the **trachea** in a transverse section?
back: The largest airway, with incomplete **C-shaped** rings of cartilage and a lining of ciliated epithelium with goblet cells.

front: How does a **bronchus** differ in appearance from the trachea?
back: It is **smaller**, and its cartilage forms **irregular blocks** rather than complete C-shaped rings.

front: How can you recognise a **bronchiole**?
back: A small airway with **no cartilage**; its wall is mostly **smooth muscle** with a thin ciliated lining.

front: How can you recognise **alveoli** in a section?
back: Clusters of many tiny, **thin-walled air sacs** appearing as small spaces, surrounded by capillaries.

front: What is a **plan diagram** (tissue map) of an airway?
back: A diagram showing only the **outline and distribution of the tissues** in a section, with **no individual cells** drawn.

front: In the trachea, the cartilage is arranged as incomplete, <u>     </u> rings.
back: In the trachea, the cartilage is arranged as incomplete, **C-shaped** rings.

front:
**True or False?**

Bronchioles contain rings of cartilage in their walls.
back:
**False.**

Bronchioles have no cartilage; this helps distinguish them from the trachea and bronchi.

front: In a **plan diagram** of the **trachea or bronchus wall**, which tissue layers are drawn, from the lumen outwards?
back:
From the lumen outwards: **ciliated epithelium** (with goblet cells) → **smooth muscle** → **cartilage** → **connective tissue**.

The trachea shows **C-shaped** cartilage rings; the bronchus shows **blocks** of cartilage.

front: What is the function of **goblet cells**?
back: They secrete **mucus**, which traps dust, microbes and **pathogens** in the airways.

front: What is the function of **ciliated epithelial cells**?
back: Their **cilia** beat to sweep **mucus** and trapped particles up towards the throat, where it is swallowed.

front: What is the function of **mucous glands** in the airways?
back: They secrete **mucus** that traps particles and pathogens, helping to keep the gas exchange system healthy.

front: What is the function of **cartilage** in the gas exchange system?
back: It **supports** the airways and holds them **open**, preventing collapse when air pressure falls during inhalation.

front: What is the function of **smooth muscle** in the airways?
back: It **contracts** to narrow the airway, controlling its diameter and the flow of air.

front: What is the function of **elastic fibres** in the airways?
back:
**Elastic fibres** stretch when the airway expands and **recoil** when the **smooth muscle relaxes**.

This returns the airway to its original diameter and helps to **force air out** during exhalation.

front: How does the **squamous epithelium** of the alveoli aid its function?
back: It is extremely **thin**, providing a **short diffusion distance** for gases.

front: The beating of <u>   </u> moves mucus and trapped particles up towards the throat.
back: The beating of **cilia** moves mucus and trapped particles up towards the throat.

front:
**True or False?**

Goblet cells move mucus towards the throat.
back:
**False.**

Goblet cells secrete mucus; it is the beating cilia of ciliated cells that move the mucus.

front: Which gas moves from the **alveoli into the blood**, and which moves the other way?
back: **Oxygen** diffuses from the alveoli into the blood; **carbon dioxide** diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.

front: By what process are gases exchanged between the alveoli and the blood?
back: By **diffusion**, with each gas moving down its own **concentration (diffusion) gradient**.

front: Why does **oxygen** diffuse from the alveoli into the blood?
back: Blood in the capillaries has a **lower** oxygen concentration than the alveolar air, so oxygen diffuses down its gradient into the blood.

front: How does a **short diffusion distance** speed up gas exchange in the alveoli?
back: The alveolar (squamous) epithelium and capillary wall are both very **thin**, so gases diffuse only a short distance.

front: How does the large number of alveoli aid gas exchange?
back: They provide a very large **surface area** for diffusion.

front: How does the **capillary network** help maintain gas exchange?
back: Continuous blood flow keeps the **concentration gradients** for oxygen and carbon dioxide steep.

front: Gases are exchanged between the alveoli and the blood by the process of <u>     </u>.
back: Gases are exchanged between the alveoli and the blood by the process of **diffusion**.

front: Define **pathogen**.
back: A **pathogen** is an organism that causes **disease**.

front: Define **infectious disease**.
back: An **infectious disease** is a disease caused by a **pathogen** that can be **transmitted** from one host to another.

front: What causes **cholera**, and what type of pathogen is it?
back: Cholera is caused by the **bacterium** **Vibrio cholerae**.

front: What causes **malaria**, and what type of pathogen is it?
back:
Malaria is caused by **protoctists** of the genus **Plasmodium**:

**Plasmodium falciparum**, **P. malariae**, **P. ovale** and **P. vivax**.

front: What causes **tuberculosis (TB)**, and what type of pathogen is it?
back: TB is caused by the **bacteria** **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** and **Mycobacterium bovis**.

front: What causes **HIV/AIDS**, and what type of pathogen is it?
back: HIV/AIDS is caused by a **virus** — the **human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)**.

front: Infectious diseases are caused by <u>     </u> and can be transmitted between hosts.
back: Infectious diseases are caused by **pathogens** and can be transmitted between hosts.

front:
**True or False?**

Malaria is caused by a bacterium.
back:
**False.**

Malaria is caused by **protoctists** of the genus **Plasmodium**.

front: Define **vector** (in disease transmission).
back: A **vector** is an organism that carries a **pathogen** from one host to another without getting the disease itself.

front: How is **cholera** transmitted?
back: By the **faecal–oral route**: drinking **water** or eating **food** contaminated with faeces containing **Vibrio cholerae**.

front: How is **malaria** transmitted?
back:
By a **vector** — the female **Anopheles** mosquito — which passes **Plasmodium** into the blood when it bites.

It can also spread through infected **blood** and across the **placenta**.

front: How is **tuberculosis (TB)** transmitted?
back: Through the **air**: inhaling **droplets** containing the bacteria when an infected person **coughs** or **sneezes**.

front: How is **HIV** transmitted?
back:
In **body fluids**:

- unprotected **sexual** contact
- infected **blood** or sharing **needles**
- from mother to child across the **placenta**, during birth, or in **breast milk**

front: Malaria is transmitted by a vector, the female <u>     </u> mosquito.
back: Malaria is transmitted by a vector, the female **Anopheles** mosquito.

front:
**True or False?**

TB is transmitted through contaminated water.
back:
**False.**

TB is spread through the **air** in droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes. **Cholera** is the disease spread through contaminated water.

front: Name the three types of factor considered in the **prevention and control** of disease.
back: **Biological**, **social** and **economic** factors.

front: How can **cholera** be prevented and controlled?
back:
Provide **clean, treated drinking water** and proper **sewage/sanitation**.

Good **hygiene**, **oral rehydration** to treat cases, and **vaccination**.

front: How can **malaria** be prevented and controlled?
back:
Control the **mosquito vector** with insecticides and by draining **stagnant water**.

Use insecticide-treated **bed nets** and **antimalarial drugs**.

front: How can **TB** be prevented and controlled?
back:
**BCG vaccination**, **contact tracing** and testing, and a full course of **antibiotics**.

Improving **living conditions** to reduce overcrowding.

front: How can **HIV** be prevented and controlled?
back:
Use **condoms**, **needle-exchange** schemes and **screening of blood**.

**Education** and contact tracing; **antiretroviral drugs** also reduce transmission.

front: Insecticide-treated <u>  </u> nets help prevent malaria by stopping mosquito bites at night.
back: Insecticide-treated **bed** nets help prevent malaria by stopping mosquito bites at night.

front:
**True or False?**

There is currently a vaccine that gives full protection against HIV.
back:
**False.**

There is no effective vaccine for HIV. Control relies on **prevention** and **antiretroviral drugs**.

front: Define **antibiotic**.
back: An **antibiotic** is a chemical, made by microorganisms, that **kills** or **inhibits the growth** of bacteria.

front: How does **penicillin** act on bacteria?
back:
It **prevents the synthesis of cross-links** in the bacterial **cell wall**.

The weakened wall cannot withstand the pressure as **water enters by osmosis**, so the cell **bursts (lysis)**.

front: Why does penicillin only affect **actively growing** bacteria?
back:
Penicillin stops **new cell wall** material from forming.

Only dividing cells are building new wall, so cells that are **not growing** are unaffected.

front: Why do **antibiotics not affect viruses**?
back:
Viruses have **no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolic machinery** of their own — they use the **host cell's**.

Antibiotics target **bacterial structures and processes** that viruses do not have.

front: Penicillin works by weakening the bacterial cell <u>  </u>, causing the cell to burst.
back: Penicillin works by weakening the bacterial cell **wall**, causing the cell to burst.

front:
**True or False?**

Antibiotics can be used to treat HIV.
back:
**False.**

HIV is a **virus**, and antibiotics only work against **bacteria**.

front: Define **antibiotic resistance**.
back: **Antibiotic resistance** is when bacteria are able to **survive exposure** to an antibiotic that would normally kill them.

front: How does antibiotic resistance **arise** in a population of bacteria?
back:
A random **mutation** gives some bacteria a **resistance allele**.

When the antibiotic is used, resistant bacteria **survive and reproduce** (natural selection), so the resistant type becomes **more common**.

front: How can resistance genes **spread between** bacteria?
back: By the transfer of **plasmids** carrying the resistance gene (conjugation), so resistance can pass even between **different species** of bacteria.

front: Antibiotic resistance first arises by a random <u>     </u> in bacterial DNA.
back: Antibiotic resistance first arises by a random **mutation** in bacterial DNA.

front:
**True or False?**

Using antibiotics creates the mutations that make bacteria resistant.
back:
**False.**

Mutations occur **randomly**. The antibiotic does not cause them — it **selects for** bacteria that are already resistant.

front: What are the main **consequences** of antibiotic resistance?
back:
Infections become **harder or impossible to treat**.

Illnesses last longer and spread more, causing **more deaths**, **higher healthcare costs**, and making routine **surgery riskier**.

front: What steps can **doctors and patients** take to reduce antibiotic resistance?
back:
Only **prescribe antibiotics when necessary** (not for viral infections).

Always **finish the full course**, and use the **correct, specific antibiotic**.

front: Besides careful prescribing, what steps reduce the **spread** of resistance?
back:
Good **hygiene** and **isolating** infected patients in hospitals.

Reducing antibiotic use in **agriculture**, and **rotating** the types of antibiotic used.

front: To reduce resistance, patients should always complete the full <u>    </u> of antibiotics.
back: To reduce resistance, patients should always complete the full **course** of antibiotics.

front:
**True or False?**

Antibiotics should be prescribed for a cold or flu.
back:
**False.**

Colds and flu are caused by **viruses**, so antibiotics have no effect. Prescribing them only encourages **resistance**.

front: Define **phagocytosis**.
back: **Phagocytosis** is the process by which a **phagocyte** engulfs and digests a **pathogen** or foreign particle.

front: What are the two main types of **phagocyte**?
back: **Neutrophils** and **macrophages**.

front: Describe the **mode of action** of a phagocyte.
back:
The phagocyte is **attracted** to the pathogen and recognises its antigens as **non-self**.

It **engulfs** the pathogen by endocytosis, enclosing it in a vesicle called a **phagosome**.

**Lysosomes** fuse with the phagosome and release **hydrolytic enzymes**.

The enzymes **digest** the pathogen.

front: How do **neutrophils** and **macrophages** differ?
back:
**Neutrophils** are short-lived and act quickly, travelling to sites of infection.

**Macrophages** are larger and longer-lived, and after engulfing a pathogen they display its antigens to help activate lymphocytes.

front: Define **phagosome**.
back: A **phagosome** is the **vesicle** formed around a pathogen after it has been engulfed by a phagocyte.

front: After a pathogen is engulfed, lysosomes fuse with the phagosome and release <u>           </u> to digest it.
back: After a pathogen is engulfed, lysosomes fuse with the phagosome and release **hydrolytic enzymes** to digest it.

front: Where are **phagocytes** produced?
back: Phagocytes are white blood cells made in the **bone marrow**.

front:
**True or False?**

Both neutrophils and macrophages become antigen-presenting cells.
back:
**False.**

Only **macrophages** display the pathogen's **antigens** to activate lymphocytes; **neutrophils** destroy the pathogen completely.

front: Define **antigen**.
back: An **antigen** is a molecule (usually a **protein** or glycoprotein) on the surface of a cell that the immune system recognises and that can **stimulate an immune response**.

front: What is the difference between **self** and **non-self** antigens?
back:
**Self antigens** are the body's **own** antigens and do **not** stimulate an immune response.

**Non-self antigens** are **foreign** (e.g. on pathogens) and **trigger** an immune response.

front: Antigens found on an organism's own cells are called <u>  </u> antigens.
back: Antigens found on an organism's own cells are called **self** antigens.

front: Give examples of things that carry **non-self** antigens.
back: **Pathogens** such as bacteria and viruses, and cells or tissue from **another organism** (e.g. a transplant).

front:
**True or False?**

Self antigens stimulate an immune response.
back:
**False.**

Self antigens are recognised as belonging to the body, so they do **not** trigger an immune response; only non-self antigens do.

front: Define **primary immune response**.
back: The **immune response** that occurs on the body's **first** exposure to a particular antigen.

front: What is the role of **macrophages** in the immune response?
back: They engulf pathogens and display the pathogen's **antigens** on their surface, becoming **antigen-presenting cells** that activate lymphocytes.

front: What is the role of **T-helper cells**?
back: They recognise antigens on antigen-presenting cells and release **cytokines** that stimulate **B-lymphocytes** and other cells to carry out the immune response.

front: What is the role of **T-killer cells**?
back: They attach to and **destroy** body cells that are **infected** with a pathogen, such as virus-infected cells.

front: What is the role of **B-lymphocytes** in the immune response?
back: When activated, they divide to form **plasma cells**, which secrete large numbers of **antibodies** specific to the antigen.

front: Define **plasma cell**.
back: A **plasma cell** is a cell derived from a **B-lymphocyte** that secretes **antibodies**.

front: Outline the sequence of events in a **primary immune response**.
back:
A **macrophage** engulfs the pathogen and displays its antigens (antigen-presenting cell).

**T-helper cells** recognise the antigens and release **cytokines**.

This activates specific **B-lymphocytes**, which divide into **plasma cells**.

Plasma cells secrete **antibodies**, and some cells become **memory cells**.

front: Activated B-lymphocytes divide to form plasma cells, which secrete <u>      </u>.
back: Activated B-lymphocytes divide to form plasma cells, which secrete **antibodies**.

front: Define **memory cell**.
back: **Memory cells** are long-lived lymphocytes produced after an immune response that **remain** in the body and respond rapidly if the same antigen is met again.

front: What is the **secondary immune response**?
back: The **faster** and **stronger** immune response that occurs on the **second** (and later) exposure to the same antigen.

front: Why is the secondary immune response faster than the primary response?
back: **Memory cells** specific to the antigen are already present, so they divide **rapidly** into plasma cells and produce antibodies much more quickly.

front: How do memory cells provide **long-term immunity**?
back: They persist in the body for **years**, so if the same pathogen returns it is destroyed **before** it can cause symptoms.

front: The response on a second exposure to an antigen is faster and stronger and is called the <u>     </u> immune response.
back: The response on a second exposure to an antigen is faster and stronger and is called the **secondary** immune response.

front: Compare antibody production in the **primary** and **secondary** responses.
back:
**Primary:** antibodies produced **slowly** and in **smaller** amounts.

**Secondary:** antibodies produced **rapidly** and in **larger** amounts.

front:
**True or False?**

Memory cells secrete antibodies.
back:
**False.**

Memory cells do not secrete antibodies; they divide rapidly into **plasma cells**, which secrete the antibodies.

front: Define **antibody**.
back: An **antibody** is a **glycoprotein** (immunoglobulin) made by **plasma cells** that binds specifically to a particular **antigen**.

front: Describe the **structure** of an antibody.
back:
An **antibody** is made of **four polypeptide chains** — two **heavy** and two **light** chains — held together by **disulfide bonds** in a **Y-shape**.

It has two **antigen-binding sites**.

front: What is the **variable region** of an antibody and why is it important?
back: The **variable region** has a specific shape that is **complementary** to one particular antigen, so each antibody binds to only **one** type of antigen.

front: Define **antigen-antibody complex**.
back: An **antigen-antibody complex** is the structure formed when an **antibody** binds to its specific **antigen**.

front: How does having **two antigen-binding sites** relate to an antibody's function?
back: An antibody can bind **two pathogens** at once, clumping them together (**agglutination**) so that phagocytes can engulf them more easily.

front: What is the role of the **constant region** of an antibody?
back: The **constant region** allows the antibody to **bind to receptors** on phagocytes, helping them to recognise and engulf the pathogen.

front: The variable region of an antibody has a shape that is <u>        </u> to a specific antigen.
back: The variable region of an antibody has a shape that is **complementary** to a specific antigen.

front:
**True or False?**

Each antibody can bind several different types of antigen.
back:
**False.**

The **variable region** is **complementary** to only **one** antigen, so each antibody binds just one type.

front: Define **monoclonal antibody**.
back: **Antibodies** that are all **identical** because they are produced by **cloned cells** derived from a single B-lymphocyte, so they bind to one specific **antigen**.

front: Define **hybridoma**.
back: A cell made by **fusing** a **B-lymphocyte** with a **tumour (myeloma) cell**; it produces antibodies and can divide indefinitely.

front: Outline the **hybridoma method** for producing monoclonal antibodies.
back:
An animal (e.g. a mouse) is **injected** with an antigen so it makes **B-lymphocytes** that produce the required antibody.

These B-lymphocytes are **fused** with **tumour (myeloma) cells** to form **hybridoma** cells.

Hybridomas making the required antibody are **selected** and **cultured**.

They **divide** to produce large amounts of identical **monoclonal antibodies**.

front: Why are B-lymphocytes fused with **tumour (myeloma) cells**?
back: B-lymphocytes do not divide well in culture, but tumour cells **divide rapidly and indefinitely**, so the hybridoma can both make antibody **and** keep dividing.

front: A hybridoma is made by fusing a B-lymphocyte with a <u>    </u> cell.
back: A hybridoma is made by fusing a B-lymphocyte with a **tumour** cell.

front: Why are the antibodies produced described as **monoclonal**?
back: They are all **identical** and specific to **one antigen**, because they are made by **clones** of a single hybridoma cell.

front: Outline the principle of using monoclonal antibodies in the **diagnosis** of disease.
back:
A monoclonal antibody is made to **bind specifically** to an antigen linked to the disease.

Attaching a **marker** (e.g. a dye or radioactive label) then shows **whether** or **where** that antigen is present.

front: How can monoclonal antibodies be used to **locate** cancer cells or blood clots?
back: The antibodies are made to bind to **antigens** on the target cells and carry a **radioactive or fluorescent marker**, so the site can be **detected** by scanning.

front: Outline the principle of using monoclonal antibodies in the **treatment** of disease.
back: They are made to bind specifically to a target (e.g. antigens on **cancer cells**), so they can **block** its activity or **deliver a drug** directly to it.

front: What is a **"magic bullet"**?
back: A **monoclonal antibody** with a **drug or toxin attached** that delivers the drug only to **target cells** (e.g. cancer cells), reducing damage to healthy cells.

front: Why do monoclonal antibody treatments cause **fewer side effects** than some other treatments?
back: Because each antibody binds to only **one specific antigen**, they target **only** the diseased cells, so healthy cells are largely **unaffected**.

front: Monoclonal antibodies are highly specific because each one binds to a single type of <u>    </u>.
back: Monoclonal antibodies are highly specific because each one binds to a single type of **antigen**.

front: Define **active immunity**.
back: Immunity gained when the body's own immune system is **stimulated by an antigen** to make its **own antibodies** and **memory cells**.

front: Define **passive immunity**.
back: Immunity gained by receiving **antibodies** made by **another** organism; no memory cells are made, so it is **short-lived**.

front: What is the difference between **natural** and **artificial** immunity?
back:
**Natural** immunity is gained through **normal life**, e.g. an infection or antibodies from the mother.

**Artificial** immunity is gained through **medical intervention**, e.g. vaccination or an injection of antibodies.

front: Give an example of **natural active** immunity.
back: Making your **own antibodies** and memory cells after **catching** and recovering from an infection.

front: Give an example of **artificial passive** immunity.
back: Being **injected with antibodies** made by another organism, e.g. anti-venom or tetanus antibodies.

front: Why is **passive** immunity short-lived while **active** immunity is long-lasting?
back:
Passive immunity provides only ready-made antibodies and **no memory cells**, so it ends when they break down.

Active immunity produces **memory cells**, giving long-term protection.

front: Immunity gained by receiving ready-made antibodies from another organism is called <u>    </u> immunity.
back: Immunity gained by receiving ready-made antibodies from another organism is called **passive** immunity.

front: Give an example of **natural passive** immunity.
back: A baby receiving antibodies from its mother across the **placenta** or in **breast milk**.

front: Define **vaccine**.
back: A preparation containing **antigens** that stimulates the immune system to produce **antibodies** and **memory cells** without causing the disease.

front: How does a vaccine provide **long-term immunity**?
back:
The vaccine's **antigens** stimulate a **primary immune response**, producing **antibodies** and **memory cells**.

If the real pathogen later enters, **memory cells** trigger a rapid **secondary response**, destroying it before symptoms develop.

front: What do vaccines contain?
back: **Antigens**, e.g. from a **weakened (attenuated)**, **dead**, or otherwise modified pathogen, or purified antigen molecules.

front: Vaccines work because they contain <u>     </u> that stimulate an immune response.
back: Vaccines work because they contain **antigens** that stimulate an immune response.

front: Why doesn't a vaccine make you ill, even though it triggers an immune response?
back: It contains only **antigens** or **weakened/dead** pathogens, which **cannot cause the disease** but still stimulate the immune system.

front:
**True or False?**

Vaccines contain live, fully active pathogens.
back:
**False.**

Vaccines contain **antigens** from dead, weakened or modified pathogens, so they cannot cause the disease.

front: Define **herd immunity**.
back: When a **large proportion** of a population is **immune** (e.g. vaccinated), so the pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting even those who are **not immune**.

front: How do vaccination programmes control the spread of an infectious disease?
back: By making most of the population **immune**, there are **fewer people** who can catch and pass on the pathogen, so **transmission** is reduced and outbreaks are prevented (**herd immunity**).

front: Why must a **high percentage** of the population be vaccinated for a programme to work?
back: So that too few **susceptible** individuals remain for the pathogen to spread between, breaking the **chain of transmission**.

front: When enough people are vaccinated, unvaccinated people are also protected; this is called <u>  </u> immunity.
back: When enough people are vaccinated, unvaccinated people are also protected; this is called **herd** immunity.

front: Why can some diseases not be easily controlled by vaccination?
back: The pathogen's **antigens change** (antigenic variation), so existing vaccines and memory cells no longer **recognise** it, e.g. influenza.

front: How did vaccination lead to the **eradication of smallpox**?
back: A **worldwide** vaccination programme made enough people immune that the virus could **no longer spread**, so smallpox was **eradicated**.
